As autonomy expands, governance complexity increases disproportionately. Industry development practices have largely prioritized capability and automation speed, while accountability architecture often remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes the Autonomy Accountability Framework, a governance model for understanding and managing accountability in autonomous AI agent systems. The framework introduces five core constructs: the Autonomy-Accountability Curve, the Agent Accountability Gap (AAG), Governance Debt (GD), the Agent Accountability Stack (AAS), and the Autonomy Accountability Index (AAI). Together they describe the structural governance challenges created by autonomous systems and outline an operational architecture for addressing them. The framework is operationalized through the Autonomy Accountability Index (AAI), a governance evaluation model designed to measure the maturity of accountability infrastructure within agent systems. AAI provides a structured lens for assessing governance readiness as autonomy scales. This work proposes a foundation for governance standards in autonomous AI agent systems and establishes a methodology for future benchmarking and ecosystem analysis. The framework can also be interpreted as a governance maturity model describing how accountability infrastructure must evolve as autonomous AI systems scale.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6391521\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6392459\", \"title\": [\"AEGIS: Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard — A Survey and Reference Architecture for AI Agent Action Accountability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As organizations deploy AI agents to execute tasks in business proces…

The framework can also be interpreted as a governance maturity model describing how accountability infrastructure must evolve as autonomous AI systems scale.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6391521\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6392459\", \"title\": [\"AEGIS: Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard — A Survey and Reference Architecture for AI Agent Action Accountability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>As organizations deploy AI agents to execute tasks in business processes, to our knowledge, no systematic academic framework exists for recording, verifying, and ensuring accountability for their actions. This study surveys industrial challenges and regulatory trends in AI agent action recording, formalizes a threat model (T1–T8), and constructs a seven-dimension evaluation framework (D1–D7). Through systematic survey of 16 academic papers and 5 industry projects and comparison matrix analysis, it identifies research gaps and demonstrates the non-substitutability of architectural differences against the two closest existing works (PROV-AGENT, InALign). The survey confirms that \\\"a cryptographically verifiable, independent third-party recording standard for AI agent runtime behavior across platforms\\\" remains an open research problem not addressed by the surveyed works. This paper proposes AEGIS (Agent Execution Governance and Integrity Standard), a three-layer reference architecture targeting these requirements, and evaluates it through a reference implementation across metrics M1–M6 and scenarios S1–S5.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6392459\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9781003747567-6\", \"title\": [\"Regulatory frameworks for AI and ESG reporting\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003747567-6\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 8, 18]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7082358\", \"title\": [\"Autonomous Governance Intelligence: An AI-Native Framework for Continuous Democratic Visibility and Accountability\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Governance intelligence should be treated as a continuous state-estimation problem rather than a complaint-resolution problem. Traditional civic technology platforms operate on transactional, complaint-centric architectures that process citizen grievances as isolated tickets. While effective for administrative workflow management, these systems often fail to generate a comprehensive understanding of broader governance conditions, disconnect citizen participation from collective impact, and prioritize procedural activity over measurable public outcomes. This paper introduces IndiaOS, a theoretical AI-native governance framework designed to transition from fragmented grievance management toward continuous governance intelligence. At the center of the framework is the Autonomous Governance Intelligence Layer (AGIL), a multi-engine architecture that continuously ingests decentralized civic observations and transforms them into structured public issues through semantic, spatial, and temporal clustering mechanisms. By establishing a clear separation between private citizen inputs and public issue outputs, the framework reduces informational fragmentation while enabling large-scale aggregation of civic signals. The model further introduces a dual-state evaluation framework that distinguishes between Official Status, representing institutional claims of resolution, and Reality Status, representing continuously verified ground-level conditions. Through multi-source evidence aggregation and dynamic accountability assessment, the architecture seeks to provide a more accurate representation of governance performance than traditional complaint-management systems. The paper argues that artificial intelligence can evolve beyond stateless generative applications toward persistent, stateful monitoring systems capable of supporting transparency, accountability, and evidence-based democratic governance. Author Ashnik X. Chaudhary is a mechanical engineering student, independent researcher, and founder exploring the application of artificial intelligence to governance, civic participation, and institutional accountability. His current work focuses on IndiaOS, an AI-native governance intelligence framework designed to transform decentralized citizen observations into continuous public visibility and evidence-based accountability systems. His broader interests include collective intelligence, digital democracy, public-sector innovation, and emerging technology policy.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7082358\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "672013eadcb3b6d607f1d351b56d507d3a2c31e7989d5cdde1108dcfaa110a40", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6391521", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6392459", "doi:10.4324/9781003747567-6", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7082358"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6391521", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6392459", "https://doi.org/10.4324/9781003747567-6", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7082358"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
